name: Jahangir Khan
one_line: Unbeaten in professional squash for five years and 555 matches - the longest winning streak in top-level sport.

facts.claim: won 555 consecutive matches, unbeaten from 1981 to 1986 - recorded by Guinness World Records as the longest winning streak by any athlete in top-level professional sport
facts.note: Wikipedia verbatim: 'the longest winning streak by any athlete in top-level professional sport as recorded by Guinness World Records.' Attribute the count to Guinness if pressed - some squash historians argue the true match count is unknowable, but Guinness canonized 555.

facts.claim: the streak ended at the 1986 World Open final, when Ross Norman beat him 5-9, 7-9, 9-7, 1-9
won the World Open in 1981 aged 17, the youngest-ever winner; world amateur champion at 15
facts.note: The streak began weeks after that 1981 title.
The British Open was squash's Wimbledon. Ten in a row.

facts.claim: his older brother Torsam died suddenly in November 1979, mid-match, at a tournament in Adelaide; Jahangir, then 15, considered quitting and instead built his career as a tribute to him
facts.note: Wikipedia: the death 'profoundly affected Khan. He considered quitting the game, but decided to pursue a career in the sport as a tribute to his brother.' Report flat, no melodrama - the facts carry it.

facts.claim: the next-longest unbeaten streak in professional sport is Esther Vergeer's 470 - the subject of an earlier video on this channel
facts.note: IPC on Vergeer: her 470 was 'second only to Pakistani squash great Jahangir Khan's record mark of 555.' Chart: gold 555 vs gray 470. Possible self-reference in script/description.

facts.claim: in 1982, mid-streak, he won the final of the ISPA Championship without losing a single point
facts.note: PSA (the professional tour itself) and olympics.com both carry it. Phrase as 'a professional final' - it was the FINAL without a point, not the whole tournament. This is the hook's 'craziest part' payoff.

comparison.second_label: the next-longest streak in sport (Esther Vergeer)
comparison.gap_description: 555 straight wins over five years; nothing else in professional sport has passed 470.

story_beat: In November 1979 his older brother Torsam, also a professional, collapsed and died mid-match in Adelaide. Jahangir was 15 and nearly quit. Two years later he was world champion at 17 - and then didn't lose a match to anyone, anywhere, for five years.
